questions.body: When finding two numbers in a sorted array that sum to a target value, what is the optimal time and space complexity using the two-pointer technique?
questions.keyPoints: Pointers at both ends converging inward achieve O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

options.text: Time: O(N), Space: O(1)
options.explanation: Starting one pointer at the left end and one at the right end of a sorted array and moving them inward based on the comparison of the current sum against target takes linear time O(N) and constant space O(1).

options.text: Time: O(N log N), Space: O(N)
options.explanation: Sorting takes O(N log N), but given that the array is already sorted, the two-pointer scan itself is O(N) time and O(1) space.

options.text: Time: O(N^2), Space: O(1)
options.explanation: O(N^2) is the brute-force nested loop approach.

options.text: Time: O(log N), Space: O(log N)
options.explanation: A linear scan inspecting elements takes at least O(N) in the worst case.

options.explanation: Sliding window operates on contiguous subarrays/substrings where expanding the right pointer and contracting the left pointer maintains or restores a monotonic property.

options.text: The problem asks to find the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
options.explanation: Shortest path in unweighted graphs is solved using Breadth-First Search (BFS).

options.text: The problem requires finding non-contiguous subsequences.
options.explanation: Non-contiguous subsequences typically require dynamic programming or backtracking.

options.text: The array contains purely negative numbers with random access queries.
options.explanation: Sliding window is an algorithmic traversal pattern, not an array element sign constraint.

questions.body: What is the time complexity of answering multiple range sum queries `sum(L, R)` on an immutable array of size N using a Prefix Sum precomputation array?
questions.keyPoints: Precomputation in O(N), query in O(1) via prefix[R+1] - prefix[L].

options.text: Precomputation: O(N), Query: O(1)
options.explanation: Precomputing `prefix[i] = prefix[i-1] + arr[i]` takes O(N) time. Each range sum query `sum(L, R)` is answered in O(1) time as `prefix[R] - prefix[L-1]`.

options.text: Precomputation: O(1), Query: O(N)
options.explanation: That is the naive approach without precomputation.

options.text: Precomputation: O(N log N), Query: O(log N)
options.explanation: Binary Indexed Tree (Fenwick) or Segment Tree provides O(log N) queries for mutable arrays, but prefix sums for immutable arrays achieve O(1).

options.text: Precomputation: O(N^2), Query: O(1)
options.explanation: Prefix array construction is single-pass linear O(N).

questions.body: What problem does Kadane's Algorithm solve in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space?
questions.keyPoints: Maximum Subarray Sum problem.

options.text: Maximum Subarray Sum (finding the contiguous subarray having the largest sum).
options.explanation: Kadane's algorithm keeps track of `current_max = max(x, current_max + x)` and `global_max = max(global_max, current_max)` in a single linear pass.

options.text: Longest Common Subsequence between two strings.
options.explanation: LCS between two strings is solved using 2D DP in O(M*N) time.

options.text: Finding the median of two sorted arrays.
options.explanation: Median of two sorted arrays is solved using binary search in O(log(min(M, N))).

options.text: Sorting an array in linear time.

questions.body: How does the Dutch National Flag algorithm (Dijkstra) partition an array containing only values 0, 1, and 2 in a single pass?
questions.keyPoints: Three pointers: low, mid, high partition the array in O(N) time and O(1) space.

options.text: Using three pointers (`low`, `mid`, `high`) where elements before `low` are 0, elements between `low` and `mid-1` are 1, and elements after `high` are 2.
options.explanation: The three-pointer approach swaps 0s to the front (`low`), 2s to the back (`high`), and advances `mid` past 1s in a single pass with O(1) auxiliary space.

options.text: By inserting all elements into a min-heap and extracting them.
options.explanation: A heap takes O(N log N) time and O(N) space.

options.text: By counting occurrences of 0, 1, 2 in a hash table and doing two passes.
options.explanation: Counting sort does two passes; DNF does it in a single pass in-place without counting.

options.text: By recursively calling QuickSort with median-of-three pivot.
options.explanation: QuickSort has recursive stack overhead and is general-purpose.

questions.body: What does the Boyer-Moore Majority Vote algorithm find in an array, and what are its complexities?
questions.keyPoints: Finds element appearing more than N/2 times in O(N) time and O(1) space.

options.text: The majority element that appears strictly more than `floor(N/2)` times in O(N) time and O(1) space.
options.explanation: By maintaining a candidate and a counter that increments when encountering the candidate and decrements otherwise, Boyer-Moore identifies the > N/2 majority element in linear time and constant space.

options.text: The most frequent element in any array regardless of count.
options.explanation: It only works if a true majority element (> N/2) exists; arbitrary mode requires a hash map.

options.text: All elements that appear exactly twice in O(log N) time.
options.explanation: It is designed specifically for majority detection (> N/2 or > N/3 extensions).

options.text: The second largest element in O(1) time.
options.explanation: Finding second largest requires inspecting all elements (O(N)).

questions.body: Why does repeatedly concatenating single characters in a loop using standard string addition (`s += c`) in languages like Java or Python lead to O(N^2) time complexity?
questions.keyPoints: Strings are immutable; each concatenation copies the entire existing string into a newly allocated buffer.

options.text: Strings are immutable; each concatenation creates a brand new string buffer and copies all previous characters, resulting in `1 + 2 + ... + N = O(N^2)` work.
options.explanation: Because strings cannot be mutated in place, each concatenation copies the accumulated string. Using a mutable buffer like `StringBuilder` or list append (`''.join(list)`) achieves linear O(N) time.

options.text: Because string hashing takes quadratic time.
options.explanation: String hashing is O(length), not quadratic.

options.text: Because the garbage collector locks all threads during string allocation.
options.explanation: Memory copying is the algorithmic bottleneck, not GC pauses.

options.text: Because character encodings must be validated via DNS lookups.
options.explanation: Encodings are local in-memory byte representations.

questions.body: What does the Longest Prefix Suffix (LPS) array / π table in the KMP string matching algorithm represent?
questions.keyPoints: LPS[i] stores the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of pattern[0..i].

options.text: For each prefix `pattern[0..i]`, the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix of that substring.
options.explanation: The LPS array allows KMP to avoid re-examining previously matched characters upon a mismatch by skipping directly to the next viable alignment in O(N + M) total time.

options.text: The alphabetical rank of each character in the alphabet.
options.explanation: LPS is based on string self-overlap, not alphabetical order.

options.text: The frequency count of each unique character in the pattern.
options.explanation: Frequency counts are used in anagram checks, not KMP alignment.

options.text: The hash values of pattern substrings for Rabin-Karp.
options.explanation: Rabin-Karp uses rolling hashes; KMP uses deterministic state transitions via LPS.

questions.body: What technique allows the Rabin-Karp algorithm to search for a pattern in text in O(N + M) average time?
questions.keyPoints: Rolling hash function to compute the hash of the sliding window in O(1) time.

options.text: A rolling hash function that computes the hash of the next sliding window in O(1) time from the previous window's hash.
options.explanation: By updating the hash incrementally (`(old_hash - outgoing_char * base^m) * base + incoming_char`), Rabin-Karp checks window equality in O(1) average time per position.

options.text: Binary search over the text characters.
options.explanation: Text is not sorted, so binary search cannot be applied directly.

options.text: Transforming the text into a binary search tree.
options.explanation: Constructing a BST would take extra time and space.

options.text: Compressing text with Huffman encoding before searching.
options.explanation: Rabin-Karp operates on raw string hashes.

options.explanation: While expanding around centers takes O(N^2) in worst case (e.g. 'aaaaa'), Manacher's algorithm uses symmetry and previously computed palindrome radii to achieve strictly O(N) time.

questions.keyPoints: Transpose the matrix (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]), then reverse each row.

options.explanation: Reversing both rows and columns results in a 180-degree rotation, not 90 degrees.

questions.body: Why does appending an element to a dynamic array (e.g., `ArrayList` in Java, `vector` in C++, or `list` in Python) have O(1) amortized time complexity, even though resizing takes O(N)?
questions.keyPoints: Geometric doubling of capacity ensures that the total cost of copying over N insertions is O(N), averaging O(1) per insert.

options.text: Geometric capacity doubling (e.g. 2x factor) ensures that expensive resize copies occur exponentially less frequently, yielding `O(N)` total copy operations across N insertions (O(1) average).
options.explanation: The sum of resizing steps `1 + 2 + 4 + ... + N` forms a geometric series bounded by `2N`. Dividing `2N` total work by N insertions proves that each append costs O(1) amortized time.

options.text: Because memory allocation is always performed on GPU hardware.
options.explanation: Heap allocations occur in CPU system memory.

options.text: Because the array only copies the first and last elements during resize.
options.explanation: All N elements must be copied to the newly allocated memory block.

options.text: Because modern operating systems do not require contiguous memory for arrays.
options.explanation: Arrays fundamentally require contiguous memory addresses for O(1) indexing.

options.text: The index of the next vowel in the string.
options.explanation: It is a general string pattern matching algorithm.

questions.body: What standard invariant boundaries are maintained when traversing an M x N matrix in spiral order?

questions.body: How can you compute an array where `output[i]` is the product of all elements of `nums` except `nums[i]`, in O(N) time WITHOUT using the division operator?
questions.keyPoints: Two passes computing running prefix products from the left, then running suffix products from the right.

options.text: Compute running prefix products in a left-to-right pass, then multiply by running suffix products in a right-to-left pass.
options.explanation: `output[i] = (product of elements before i) * (product of elements after i)`. By computing prefix products and accumulating a running suffix product in reverse, the result is computed in O(N) time with O(1) extra space.

options.text: Multiply all elements together and divide by `nums[i]`.
options.explanation: The prompt explicitly forbids the division operator (which also fails when elements are 0).

options.text: Use nested loops to multiply all other elements for each index.
options.explanation: Nested loops take quadratic O(N^2) time.

options.text: Sort the array and take the factorial of index `i`.
options.explanation: Sorting destroys index positioning and does not compute arbitrary element products.
